Recognize that GitHub Copilot supports three repository custom-instruction types — repository-wide, path-specific, and agent instructions — and choose the type whose scope matches the guidance you want to give.
Put guidance that should apply to every request in a repository-wide file located exactly at .github/copilot-instructions.md, creating the .github directory first if it does not exist.

You may author the repository-wide instructions file from scratch or ask the Copilot cloud agent to generate it from the agents tab by selecting the target repository and submitting an onboarding prompt.
For custom instructions to affect Copilot code review, keep the code-review custom-instructions setting enabled (it is on by default) and toggle it under repository Settings > Copilot > Code review.

Recommend always-on custom instructions when a team needs standards, guidelines, or expectations applied automatically across a scope; place them at the matching scope file (.github/copilot-instructions.md repo-wide, .github/instructions/*.instructions.md path-specific, AGENTS.md for third-party agents, or org/personal settings).
Structure a repository instructions file to cover the project overview, folder structure, coding standards and conventions, and the tools/libraries/frameworks in use.
Avoid instructions that point to external resources, dictate a response style, or fix a required level of detail in large, diverse repositories, since they may not produce the intended results.
When response quality degrades, temporarily disable repository custom instructions to isolate whether the instructions are the cause.
Use organization custom instructions for organization-wide preferences such as a mandated response language, disabling code blocks, or routing certain topics to a knowledge base.

Use prompt files (*.prompt.md) for reusable, task-specific chat interactions and keep them distinct from codebase-wide custom instructions; rely on them only in IDEs that support them (VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains).
Recommend prompt files for focused single tasks run repeatedly with different inputs, stored at .github/prompts/*.prompt.md and invoked manually via chat reference or the prompt file picker.
Structure a prompt file to state its goal, ask for any missing inputs, and enumerate the concrete requirements, standards, and reference files for the task.

Account for IDE differences in supported instruction mechanisms: GitHub.com and VS Code support all three repository types; Visual Studio supports repository-wide and path-specific; Xcode uses a single .github/copilot-instructions.md; Eclipse offers workspace and project instructions.

Scope narrower guidance to matching files by adding .github/instructions/NAME.instructions.md files whose names end in .instructions.md, each beginning with an applyTo frontmatter key using glob syntax (comma-separated for multiple patterns).

Expect repository-wide and matching path-specific instructions to be combined: when a path-specific file matches the working file and a repository-wide file also exists, both sets of instructions are applied together.
Write custom instructions in natural-language Markdown; whitespace and layout between instructions are ignored, so formatting choices do not change their effect.
When onboarding a repository with cloud-agent-generated instructions, keep them under two pages and non-task-specific, and run the onboarding task only once per repository.

Control which agent consumes a path-specific file with the excludeAgent frontmatter key (value code-review or cloud-agent); omitting excludeAgent means both Copilot code review and the cloud agent use the file.
Evaluate a skill with a balanced test set: trigger tests, functional tests, and with-skill versus baseline comparisons covering reliability, efficiency, consistency, and correction burden.
Use skill-creator for drafting, structural review, trigger-risk review, and test suggestions, but keep automated testing and quantitative evaluation as separate work.
Run every test case both with the skill and against a baseline (no skill, or the previous version) so results can be compared rather than judged in isolation.

Run the evaluate sequence as one continuous flow (never via /skill-test or another testing skill), spawning each test case's with-skill and baseline runs in the same turn; choose the baseline by context -- no skill at all for a new skill, a snapshot of the old skill for an improvement.
For ordered workflows, specify step order, data dependencies, validation points, and rollback behavior explicitly.
For refinement workflows, define quality criteria, run validation, fix identified issues, repeat until a stop condition, and then finalize.
Build validation feedback loops into quality-critical workflows so the agent checks results immediately, fixes concrete failures, and repeats until the gate passes.
For context-dependent tool choice, use explicit decision criteria, fallbacks, service-specific metadata, and a short explanation of the selected path.
For domain-governed workflows, run domain checks before action, document processing decisions, and preserve an audit trail.

On difficult, policy-heavy domains, pair the think tool with an optimized prompt that gives domain-specific reasoning examples: list applicable rules, check for missing required information, verify policy compliance, and inspect tool results for correctness.
Fix overtriggering by adding negative trigger guidance, narrowing the description to the actual domain or artifact, and explicitly excluding adjacent requests that belong elsewhere.
Place thoroughness encouragement in the user prompt rather than relying on SKILL.md to change effort level.

Use a lifecycle checklist around upload: verify use cases, tools, structure, frontmatter, instructions, error handling, examples, references, trigger tests, functional tests, integration, packaging, real-conversation feedback, and version metadata.
When reporting a public skill defect, include the skill name, observed error, and reproduction steps.

Use optional frontmatter metadata deliberately for licensing, compatibility, tool access, ownership, versioning, category, documentation, and support, while treating YAML as data with no executable code.
Structure every SKILL.md as YAML frontmatter followed by a Markdown body, and ensure the frontmatter always declares the required name and description fields.
Match instruction strictness to task risk: use heuristic prose for open-ended judgment, parameterized patterns for preferred approaches, and exact commands for fragile operations.

Match instruction specificity to task fragility: give the agent freedom and explain the purpose when multiple approaches are valid and variation is tolerable, but be prescriptive and forbid deviation when operations are fragile, consistency matters, or a fixed sequence is required.
Use progressive disclosure: make SKILL.md an overview and route detailed, domain-specific, advanced, or conditional material to directly linked files.
Keep skill references one hop from SKILL.md and give long reference files a contents overview so agents can find complete relevant sections.

Use progressive disclosure: keep SKILL.md to the core instructions needed every run (under ~500 lines and ~5,000 tokens), move detailed material into references/, and tell the agent exactly when to load each file rather than giving a generic pointer.

Apply progressive disclosure: load the right context at the right time via a tree of files rather than one upfront repository — move situational instructions (verification, code review) into selectively-called skills and split long skills into multiple files.
Keep volatile or deprecated guidance out of the mainline path by separating current instructions from legacy patterns.
Give the agent a default implementation path and mention alternatives only as scoped exceptions.
Run agent-generated code only inside a governed execution environment with sandboxing, resource limits, and monitoring.

Use hooks for actions that must run deterministically with guaranteed execution at a specific point in the agent lifecycle (e.g. formatting after every edit, approving/denying tool executions, secret scanning), configured in .github/hooks/*.json.
State dependency requirements explicitly and verify them against the intended execution environment instead of assuming packages or tools are already available.

Prefer a runtime dependency-resolving tool runner (uvx, pipx, npx, bunx, deno run, go run) so a skill can invoke a tool without a manual install step, choosing the runner that matches the target runtime and its install/caching characteristics.
Design skill resources around lazy access: large references, examples, data, and scripts are acceptable when agents are guided to load or execute only the parts needed for the task.
Prefer just-in-time loading through lightweight references when the agent can retrieve targeted slices of large external information.
Keep reference files small and focused since agents load them on demand, and use assets/ only for static resources like templates, images, and data files.
Budget context as a scarce resource: include enough information for reliable behavior, but prefer the smallest high-signal set over broad accumulation.
Write system instructions at a usable altitude: concrete enough to guide behavior, but not so procedural that they become brittle.
Separate prompt guidance by purpose so background, instructions, tool guidance, and output expectations are easy for the model to locate.

Eliminate conflicting and overlapping instructions across the system prompt, skills, CLAUDE.md, and the user request; contradictory guidance forces the model to spend reasoning reconciling it before acting.
Iterate prompts from a lean baseline, adding instructions or examples only to address observed failures.

Have the initializer expand the user's high-level prompt into a comprehensive, concrete feature list of end-to-end feature descriptions, with every feature initially marked as failing, so coding agents have an explicit definition of full functionality.
Design agent tools as clear, non-overlapping, token-efficient contracts with robust behavior and unambiguous parameters.
Use few-shot examples as canonical demonstrations of desired behavior instead of stuffing prompts with exhaustive edge-case inventories.
When using autonomous runtime exploration, budget for slower progress and provide enough tool guidance to prevent wasteful searches or missed evidence.
Let model capability justify simpler scaffolding and greater autonomy, but keep the design grounded in what has been tested for the task.

Re-evaluate scaffolding whenever a more capable model ships: a stronger model needs less scaffolding, so re-examine the harness, strip pieces that are no longer load-bearing, and add pieces that unlock newly-possible capability.
For long-horizon tasks, add external continuity mechanisms rather than relying on a larger context window alone.

Design explicit mechanisms against the two dominant long-task failure modes — loss of coherence as the context window fills, and unreliable/over-generous self-evaluation — rather than assuming the model handles them.

Use context resets (spin up a fresh agent with a cleared window plus a structured state-carrying handoff), not just in-place compaction, when the model exhibits context anxiety; drop resets once a newer model sustains long context on its own.

Do not rely on context compaction alone to preserve continuity across sessions; add explicit externally-persisted state, because compaction is insufficient and does not reliably pass clear instructions to the next session.

Avoid irreversible retain/discard context decisions on long-horizon tasks (compaction, trimming): store context as an interrogable object outside the context window, since it is hard to know which tokens future turns need and compacted context is unrecoverable unless it was stored.

Use the durable session log as the external context object and expose positional-slice interrogation (e.g. getEvents) so the brain can resume where it stopped, rewind before a moment, or reread context before an action.

Separate durable context storage (the session's job) from context management and transformation (the harness's job, e.g. organizing context for prompt-cache hits), because the specific context engineering future models will need cannot be predicted; guarantee only that the session is durable and interrogable.
Treat the context window as the primary constraint: it fills fast and model performance degrades as it fills, so actively manage what enters it.
Manage context aggressively: /clear between unrelated tasks, rely on and steer auto-compaction, use /compact <instructions> for control, and /btw for side questions that should not enter history.
Design compaction to retain critical state first, then remove redundancy after recall has been protected.
Clear stale raw tool outputs when their exact details are no longer needed, while retaining the conclusions or state required for later work.
When enabling code-driven tool use, explicitly opt in only appropriate tools and keep their raw results inside the code-execution flow until the final output is ready.
Use structured notes as external memory for project state, progress, dependencies, and decisions that must survive context resets.
Start tool development with a quick prototype, real integration testing, relevant implementation documentation, and direct user/workflow feedback before hardening the design.
Evaluate tool quality with realistic workflow tasks, realistic data, verifiable outcomes, and verifiers tolerant of harmless output variation.
Collect diagnostic feedback, raw transcripts, and operational metrics because accuracy alone can hide why tool use succeeds or fails.

Use recurring evaluation symptoms to guide concrete tool revisions: redundant calls point toward response sizing controls, while invalid inputs point toward clearer descriptions, schemas, or examples.

Choose the think tool for complex tool use, careful analysis of outputs across long tool-call chains, detailed policy navigation, and sequential decisions where earlier choices constrain later ones and mistakes are costly.
Do not make evaluations depend on one prescribed tool-use path when several valid strategies could solve the task.
Use held-out evaluations whenever agents or humans optimize tools against training examples, so improvements are checked for generalization.

Make owning and iterating on evaluations as routine as maintaining unit tests, because teams can waste weeks on AI features that 'work' in early testing but fail unstated expectations a good eval would surface early.

Understand each evaluation method's trade-offs before relying on it: automated evals give fast, reproducible, no-user-impact iteration but need maintenance and can create false confidence; production monitoring gives ground truth but is reactive and noisy; A/B testing measures real outcomes and controls confounds but is slow and needs traffic; user feedback surfaces unanticipated problems but is sparse and skewed; manual transcript review builds intuition but doesn't scale; human studies are gold-standard but expensive and slow.
Keep the tool surface selective: build a small number of high-impact tools with clear, distinct purposes before expanding the set.
Prefer targeted or workflow-level tools over broad list endpoints when they reduce irrelevant context or combine commonly chained operations behind one coherent action.
Use programmatic tool calling for workflows where code can reduce context bloat, inference round-trips, or fragile manual synthesis.
Namespace tools to make service, resource, and domain boundaries legible, and choose the naming pattern from evaluation evidence rather than universal convention.
Return only high-signal context by default, using semantic names or simple interpretable identifiers unless technical IDs are needed for a follow-up action.
Choose tool response formats through evaluation because XML, JSON, Markdown, or other structures may perform differently by task and model.
Protect the agent context budget with pagination, filtering, range selection, truncation, sensible defaults, and narrowing guidance when outputs are shortened.

Keep script output size predictable (default to a summary or limit and support pagination via --offset or an explicit --output flag) because many agent harnesses truncate output beyond roughly 10-30K characters.
Make tool validation failures actionable by explaining the required correction or expected input shape instead of returning opaque errors or raw tracebacks.

Engineer tool descriptions and schemas as part of the prompt: include domain context, query syntax, terminology, resource relationships, strict models, and unambiguous parameter names, then measure description changes with evaluations.
Make tool discovery text explicit: use capability-specific names and descriptions, and tell the model what broad tool domains can be searched.
Use tool input examples to teach conventions that schemas cannot express, including optional-field patterns, nested object usage, correlated parameters, and similar-tool disambiguation.

Design expressive tool, script, and file interfaces (clear, self-describing parameters) instead of supplying usage examples, because examples can constrain a capable model to a narrow exploration space.

Prefer high-fidelity references — code, detailed test suites, functions to port, and HTML artifacts/mockups — over prose descriptions or screenshots, and @-mention them so the model can consult in-depth information for the current plan.
Use deferred tool discovery for large tool libraries so the model loads only the tool definitions needed for the current task.
Configure deferred tool libraries with a small always-loaded core and a searchable long tail.

When a dedicated tool returns skill content, wrap it in identifying tags (so it is distinguishable and preservable during compaction) and enumerate bundled resources without eagerly reading them, letting the model load specific files on demand.

Expose many tools cheaply through deferred loading: keep full tool definitions out of context and require the agent to fetch them via ToolSearch before use, so tool count does not inflate the always-on context.
Document programmatically called tools with clear return shapes so generated orchestration code can parse, aggregate, and compare outputs reliably.
Write tool examples as concise realistic variants that show minimal, partial, and full calls only where they resolve real ambiguity.
Avoid the think tool for non-sequential, single, or parallel tool calls and for simple low-constraint instruction following, where the source reports no measurable improvement.
Choose advanced tool-use features by diagnosing the active bottleneck before layering additional mechanisms.
Start with the simplest LLM design that can solve the task, and add agentic complexity only when measured outcomes justify the added latency, cost, and operational risk.
Choose workflows for predictable predefined paths and choose autonomous agents only when flexible, model-directed control is needed for an open-ended task.
Constrain autonomous agents with checkpoints, blocker-handling, stopping conditions, sandbox testing, and guardrails because autonomy can raise cost and compound errors.
Prompt with good heuristics and explicit guardrails rather than rigid step-by-step rules, because agents legitimately take many different valid paths.
Use routing when inputs can be classified accurately into distinct categories that deserve different prompts, tools, models, or downstream processes.
Use parallelization when subtasks are independent, separate considerations need focused attention, or multiple independent judgments improve confidence.
Use an orchestrator-workers pattern when the required subtasks cannot be predicted in advance; have the orchestrator decompose, delegate, and synthesize dynamically.
Define tool formats in ways that are easy for an LLM to produce and parse: allow reasoning space, use familiar text conventions, and avoid fragile formatting overhead.
Write tool definitions with docstring-level clarity: specify parameters, examples, edge cases, and boundaries, especially when tools are similar.
Provide searchable tool discovery with adjustable detail levels when filesystem browsing alone is not enough for efficient MCP tool selection.
Avoid using the model context as a data bus for large intermediate results; move, filter, and summarize data inside the execution environment before returning model-visible output.
Implement repeat checks, waits, retries, branching, and error handling in code rather than forcing every control-flow step through the model loop.
Keep intermediate and sensitive data outside the model context by default, and expose only explicitly logged, returned, or policy-approved values.
Use client-side tokenization or equivalent data-flow controls for sensitive fields that must pass between tools without being exposed to the model.
Persist intermediate state and reusable task code in the agent workspace when workflows need resume capability, progress tracking, or repeated execution.
Default to extended thinking rather than a dedicated 'think' tool; reserve the think tool for specific complex agentic cases where extended thinking is insufficient.

Position the think tool as an in-flight reconsideration step used after generation has begun (typically after receiving tool results) and before the next action or response, not as a substitute for comprehensive up-front planning.
On easier, lower-constraint domains, simply making the think tool available may improve outcomes without additional prompt examples.
Place long or complex think-tool usage guidance in the system prompt rather than relying solely on the tool description, so the model integrates the thinking behavior into its overall conduct.

Justify adopting the think tool by task complexity rather than adding it universally, because it increases prompt length and output-token usage; its low downside holds only when it is optional and side-effect-free.
Use extended thinking as the lead agent's planning scratchpad and interleaved thinking for subagents to evaluate tool results, spot gaps, and refine the next query.
Prefer the think tool when the user query alone is insufficient and Claude must reason over external information discovered through tool-call results before acting.
Implement the think tool as a read-only, side-effect-free scratchpad: it records reasoning but must not fetch information, alter databases, or modify repositories.

Expect the think tool's benefits to improve consistency (sustained through pass^k up to k=5) and to hold across benchmarks (tau-bench and a statistically significant +1.6pp SWE-bench gain), with generalization across recent Claude generations reported but hedged.
Evaluate the agent as the harness (scaffold) and model working together, not the model in isolation, because the two jointly determine agent behaviour.
Treat harness design as a first-class lever for long-running agentic coding: the surrounding scaffold materially changes outcomes independent of the base model, so invest in it deliberately.

Grade the outcome (the final state in the environment at the end of a trial), not what the transcript claims the agent did; verify the real end state (e.g. the reservation exists in the database) rather than trusting a success message.

Read transcripts and grades from many trials regularly and invest in transcript-viewing tooling, because you cannot know whether graders work without doing so; a failed-task transcript reveals whether the agent made a genuine mistake or the grader rejected a valid solution.
Run multiple trials per task rather than a single run, because model outputs vary between runs and repetition yields more consistent, reliable measurement.

Choose grader types by trade-off: prefer deterministic code-based graders where possible (fast, cheap, reproducible, but brittle to valid variation), use model-based graders where flexibility or nuance is needed (scalable but non-deterministic and needing calibration), and use human graders judiciously for validation (gold standard but expensive and slow).
Score multidimensional success by combining graders per task—weighted (combined score must hit a threshold), binary (all must pass), or hybrid—rather than relying on a single check.

Set target pass rates by eval purpose: capability ('quality') evals should start at a low pass rate on tasks the agent struggles with, while regression evals should sit near 100% so any decline signals breakage.
Once an agent is launched and optimised, graduate high-pass-rate capability evals into a regression suite run continuously to catch drift.

Treat a 0% pass rate across many trials with frontier models (e.g. 0% pass@100) as most likely a broken task or grader, not an incapable agent, and investigate the eval before concluding the agent failed.

Watch for saturation: an eval at 100% pass rate tracks regressions but gives no signal for improvement, and near saturation large capability gains show up as small score increases (e.g. SWE-Bench Verified moved from ~30% to >80% within a year), so retire or refresh saturated evals for capability measurement.

For coding agents, rely on deterministic outcome tests (does the code run, do the tests pass) plus an LLM rubric for overall code quality, adding heuristic code-quality rules and transcript grading of tool/user interaction only as needed.

Treat resource configuration (CPU, RAM, and time limits) for agentic coding evals as a first-class experimental variable, documented and controlled with the same rigor as prompt format or sampling temperature, because infrastructure configuration alone can shift scores past leaderboard margins.

For conversational agents, evaluate the interaction itself: combine verifiable end-state outcomes, transcript constraints (e.g. finished under N turns), and LLM rubrics for task completion and interaction quality, often using a second LLM to simulate the user across multi-turn dialogue.

Evaluate computer-use and browser-use agents in a real or sandboxed environment, verifying the intended outcome through backend state rather than a confirmation page, and check that the agent selects the right interaction mode (DOM-based is fast but token-heavy; screenshot-based is slower but more token-efficient).

Select the aggregate metric by what matters: use pass@k (probability of at least one correct solution in k attempts; rises with k) when only one success is needed (e.g. pass@1 for coding), and pass^k (probability all k trials succeed; falls with k) for customer-facing agents needing consistent, reliable behaviour every time.

Start small: begin with as few as 20-50 simple tasks drawn from real observed failures rather than waiting for hundreds, because early on each system change has a large, noticeable effect so small samples suffice.

Write unambiguous tasks: a good task is one where two domain experts would independently reach the same pass/fail verdict, and everything the grader checks is clear from the task description, so agents don't fail on ambiguous specs.
Create a reference solution—a known working output that passes all graders—for each task to prove the task is solvable and to verify the graders are configured correctly.
For tasks with multiple components, build in partial credit so an agent that completes some steps scores above one that fails immediately, giving finer-grained signal.

Double-check tasks and graders before trusting low scores, because subtle failure modes—grading bugs, agent-harness constraints, or ambiguity—can produce low scores despite good agent performance (e.g. a model rose from 42% to 95% on CORE-Bench after fixing rigid grading, ambiguous specs, and non-reproducible tasks).
Write each skill's description to clearly signal the tasks it handles, because the agent matches the task against the description to decide activation and only then loads the full instructions.
Capture specialized domain expertise as reusable skill instructions and resources so agents can apply it reliably across tasks.
Build balanced problem sets that test both where a behaviour should occur and where it should not, to avoid class-imbalanced evals and the one-sided optimisation they cause.

Build a robust harness with a stable environment and isolate each trial by starting from a clean state, because unnecessary shared state (leftover files, cached data, prior git history, resource exhaustion) causes correlated failures or inflated performance and makes results unreliable.

Grade what the agent produced, not the specific path it took (e.g. an exact tool-call sequence), because checking rigid step sequences yields brittle tests that punish valid approaches the eval designer didn't anticipate.
Design evals so failures seem fair—it is clear what the agent got wrong and why—so that when scores don't climb you can be confident it is due to agent performance and not a broken eval.

Calibrate LLM-as-judge graders against human experts, give the judge an explicit way out (e.g. return 'Unknown' when it lacks information) to avoid hallucination, and use clear structured rubrics that grade each dimension with an isolated judge rather than one judge for all dimensions.

Grade free-form agent outputs with a single LLM-as-judge call that emits a 0.0-1.0 score and pass/fail against a fixed rubric (factual accuracy, citation accuracy, completeness, source quality, tool efficiency).
Make graders resistant to bypasses and hacks so that passing genuinely requires solving the problem rather than exploiting unintended loopholes.

Do not take eval scores at face value until someone digs into the details and reads transcripts; if grading is unfair, tasks are ambiguous, valid solutions are penalised, or the harness constrains the model, revise the eval before trusting it.
When an eval is flaky (passes sometimes, fails others / high stddev), tighten the skill's instructions with examples or more specific guidance to reduce interpretive ambiguity.

Treat the eval suite as a living artifact with clear ownership: a durable model is a dedicated evals team owning core infrastructure while domain experts and product teams contribute most tasks and run the evaluations themselves.

Weigh the asymmetry that a model provider can shield its eval infrastructure with dedicated hardware while external evaluators usually cannot, when comparing internally-run scores against externally-reproduced ones.

Enable the people closest to requirements and users (product managers, customer success, salespeople) to contribute eval tasks directly (e.g. as a PR), since they are best positioned to define success.

Map evaluation methods to lifecycle stages: automated evals pre-launch and in CI/CD, production monitoring post-launch for drift, A/B testing to validate significant changes once traffic suffices, ongoing user-feedback triage and weekly transcript sampling, and reserve systematic human studies for calibrating LLM graders or evaluating subjective outputs.

Layer multiple evaluation methods like a Swiss-cheese safety model, because no single layer catches every issue; the most effective teams pair automated evals for iteration, production monitoring for ground truth, and periodic human review for calibration.

When resetting context, ensure the handoff artifact carries enough prior state and next-steps for the next agent to continue cleanly, and weigh the added orchestration complexity, token overhead, and latency against the benefit.
Separate the agent that produces work from the agent that judges it; a distinct work/judge split is a strong lever for output quality even on tasks with verifiable outcomes.

Do not assume separation alone yields rigor: deliberately tune the standalone evaluator to be skeptical, since making an external judge critical is far more tractable than making a generator self-critical.

Make subjective quality gradable by encoding explicit criteria and reframing unanswerable questions ('is this good?') into criteria-anchored ones ('does this follow our principles?') the model can grade against.

Weight grading criteria toward the model's weak dimensions (e.g. design quality, originality) rather than dimensions it already handles well by default (e.g. craft, functionality), and give the same criteria to both generator and evaluator.

Give the evaluator real tools to interact with the live running artifact (e.g. a browser/Playwright MCP) before it scores, rather than grading static snapshots, accepting the added wall-clock cost per cycle.
Instruct the generator to make an explicit refine-or-pivot decision after each evaluation: refine when scores trend well, pivot to a different approach when they do not.
Treat criteria wording as prompt engineering: the exact language attached to grading criteria steers the character of the output, so choose and test that language deliberately.
Expect that well-chosen criteria and prompt language lift output above an unprompted baseline even before any feedback loop runs; do not attribute all gains to the evaluator loop.

Map the generator-evaluator loop onto the software development lifecycle — code review and QA are the evaluator role — via a planner/generator/evaluator architecture, each agent addressing a specific observed gap.

Use a planner that expands a terse prompt into an ambitious but high-level product spec, deliberately deferring granular technical detail so that early spec errors cannot cascade into downstream implementation.
Have the generator implement one feature (or sprint) at a time from the spec, self-evaluate at the end of each unit before handing off to QA, and use version control.

Have the evaluator exercise the running application through real user-like interaction (UI, API endpoints, database state) and grade each unit against both discovered bugs and explicit criteria, each with a hard threshold that fails the unit when unmet.
Negotiate a per-unit 'contract' that defines what 'done' means and how it will be verified before any code is written, to bridge a high-level spec and testable implementation.
Coordinate agents through durable file-based handoffs (one writes, another reads and responds) rather than over-specifying implementation up front.

Expect a multi-agent harness to cost substantially more than a solo run (here ~20x) and justify that cost by the quality and feature-completeness gap it closes, since the solo run's core feature was broken while the harness run worked.

Do not rely on Claude as a QA agent out of the box — it rationalizes away real issues and tests superficially; tune it iteratively from logs where its judgment diverged from yours (expect several rounds) and accept residual verification headroom.

Keep harnesses minimal — adopt 'find the simplest solution possible, add complexity only when needed' — and treat every component as an explicit, testable assumption about what the model cannot do on its own; those assumptions may be wrong and go stale as models improve.
Simplify a harness methodically: remove one component at a time and measure its impact on the result, rather than cutting back radically, so you can tell which pieces are actually load-bearing.
Remove task-decomposition constructs (e.g. sprint chunking) once the model can natively sustain coherent long-running work without them.
Keep the planner even when simplifying the harness, because without an upfront spec the generator under-scopes and produces a less feature-rich result.

Gate the evaluator on task difficulty rather than treating it as a fixed yes/no: include it when the task sits at or beyond what the model does reliably solo, and drop it as unnecessary overhead for tasks well within that boundary.

Expect recent capabilities that are thin in the model's training data (e.g. building tool-driven in-app agents) to require substantial extra prompting iteration before the model produces them correctly.
Build against the specific target model empirically: experiment directly with it, read its traces on realistic problems, and tune performance toward the desired outcome.

Store the feature list as JSON and restrict coding agents to only toggling a feature's pass/fail status; forbid adding, removing, or rewriting features or tests, using strongly-worded instructions, because the model is less likely to inappropriately overwrite JSON and edited tests hide missing functionality.
Constrain each coding session to work on a single feature at a time to counter the agent's tendency to one-shot the whole task and run out of context mid-implementation.

Require every session to end in a clean, mergeable state (no major bugs, orderly, well-documented) by committing progress to git with descriptive messages and writing a progress-file summary for the next session.

Persist a progress file alongside git history so a fresh-context agent can quickly reconstruct the state of work and use git to revert bad changes and recover working states; this also removes wasted effort re-deriving prior state.

Begin every coding session with a fixed orientation routine: confirm the working directory (pwd), read the git log and progress file, then read the feature list and pick the highest-priority not-yet-done feature.

Have the initializer write an init.sh that starts the development server, and run a basic end-to-end smoke test at the start of each session before implementing any new feature, so a broken state is detected and fixed first rather than compounded.

Require end-to-end verification with realistic, user-like tooling (e.g. browser automation) before marking a feature complete; unit tests and curl checks alone are insufficient and let the agent falsely declare features done.
Do not assume automated UI/vision testing catches every bug; account for tooling blind spots (for example, browser-native alert modals not exposed through the automation tool) when judging coverage.
Prevent premature 'declaring victory' by grounding completion in the feature list plus tested self-verification rather than the agent's impression that progress has been made.
Bake the testing and orientation routine into the harness rather than re-deriving it each session, which saves tokens and ensures consistent verification behaviour.

Treat these harness patterns as validated for full-stack web-app development and only probably-generalizable to other long-horizon domains; whether a single general-purpose agent or a specialized multi-agent architecture performs best remains an open question.

Budget for multi-agent token cost explicitly: the architecture's gains come mainly from spending more tokens across separate context windows, so expect roughly 15x chat token usage and only adopt it when task value justifies that cost.
Prefer dynamic, multi-step search that adapts to new findings over static RAG retrieval of fixed similar chunks.
Persist the lead agent's plan and essential state to external memory so it survives context-window truncation beyond ~200k tokens.
Route final outputs through a dedicated citation step that attributes every claim to its source before returning results.

Delegate with detailed task descriptions: give each subagent an explicit objective, output format, tool/source guidance, and clear boundaries, because vague delegation causes duplicated work and coverage gaps.
Delegate investigation and isolated tasks to subagents that run in their own context and report back summaries, keeping the main conversation clean.

Delegate complex subtasks that should run in isolation from the main agent to subagents (e.g. codebase research, running test suites); treat subagents as runtime processes triggered automatically or by direct reference, not as user-configured files.

Embed explicit effort-scaling rules in prompts that match agent count and tool-call budget to query complexity (e.g. 1 agent / 3-10 calls simple, 2-4 subagents / 10-15 calls comparison, 10+ subagents complex).
Iterate on agent prompts by simulating with the exact prompts and tools and watching agents step-by-step to surface concrete failure modes.
Use the model to improve itself: run a test-and-rewrite loop where an agent diagnoses failures and rewrites prompts and tool descriptions.

Write precise, context-rich prompts: reference specific files, name the scenario and testing preferences, point to source (e.g. git history) and existing patterns, and describe bug symptom + likely location + what 'fixed' looks like.
Prompt agents to search broad-to-narrow: start with short broad queries, evaluate, then progressively narrow, countering the default toward overly specific queries.
Parallelize at two levels—lead spins up 3-5 subagents concurrently and each subagent calls 3+ tools concurrently—to cut research latency dramatically.
Start evaluating immediately with a small (~20-query) set of realistic queries rather than waiting to build a large suite, since early changes have large, easily visible effects.
For agents that mutate persistent state over many turns, evaluate the correct final end-state at discrete checkpoints rather than judging each intermediate turn.
Deploy updates to long-running agents with rainbow deployments—gradually shifting traffic from old to new versions while both run—so in-flight agents are not disrupted.

Weigh synchronous vs asynchronous subagent execution deliberately: synchronous is simpler but bottlenecks on the slowest subagent and blocks steering, while asynchronous adds parallelism at the cost of harder coordination, state consistency, and error propagation.

Have subagents write outputs to an external filesystem and return lightweight references to the coordinator to avoid the lossy 'game of telephone' and reduce token overhead, especially for structured outputs.

Treat delegation and collaboration structure as the primary design lever: because multi-agent systems show emergent behavior, write prompts as collaboration frameworks that define division of labor, problem-solving approaches, and effort budgets.

Treat harness workarounds as provisional: re-test and remove them as models improve, because assumptions about what the model cannot do go stale and yesterday's fix (e.g. context resets for 'context anxiety') can become dead weight.
After patching any single shortcut the model found, re-test from scratch, because the model may still reach the intended solution through deeper analysis.

Virtualize an agent into independently swappable components -- a session (event log), a harness (the model loop and tool router), and a sandbox (code/file execution) -- defined by stable interfaces rather than by their current implementations.

Decouple the brain (model plus harness) from the hands (sandboxes and tools) and from the session (event log) so each interface assumes little about the others and can fail or be replaced independently.

Match harness topology to model capability: a single container suits weaker models, but as intelligence scales prefer connecting one brain to many hands -- which requires the model to reason about where to route work -- and allow decoupled hands to be passed between brains.

Design a meta-harness opinionated only about the interfaces around the model -- manipulating state via a session, computing via a sandbox, and scaling to many brains and many hands -- while making no assumptions about their number, location, or the specific harness in use.

Do not couple session, harness, and sandbox into one container: that 'pet' design loses the session on container failure, makes distinct failures indistinguishable, prevents safe debugging when user data is co-located, and bakes in a co-located-resource assumption that blocks connecting to a customer's own network.

Provision sandboxes lazily via a brain-issued tool call so inference can start as soon as pending events are pulled, instead of running the brain inside a container -- which forces one container per brain and makes every session pay full setup cost even when it never touches the sandbox.

Invoke every sandbox and tool through one uniform interface such as execute(name, input) -> string, so any container, custom tool, MCP server, or first-party tool is interchangeable and the harness need not know what backs it.
Treat the container as cattle: when it fails, surface the failure to the model as a tool-call error and reprovision a fresh container from a standard recipe rather than nursing the failed one.

Keep the session log outside the harness so the harness is also cattle: on crash, reboot a new harness, refetch the event log, and resume from the last event; write events durably during the loop so the run stays recoverable.

Never place credentials where the model's generated code can reach them; narrow token scoping is only a partial mitigation because it assumes model limitations that erode as models get smarter, so make tokens structurally unreachable from the sandbox.

Keep credentials out of the sandbox using resource-bundled auth or an external vault: clone Git with a token wired into the local remote at sandbox init so push/pull need no agent-held token, and route MCP calls through a proxy that resolves session-scoped credentials from a vault so the harness never sees them.

Optimize for time-to-first-token, the latency users feel most, by running many stateless harnesses connected to hands only when needed; the reference implementation measured roughly 60% lower p50 TTFT and over 90% lower p95 from lazy provisioning.

Treat every technical evaluation as perishable: re-test it against each new frontier-model release and redesign it when the model can match your strongest candidates, rather than assuming a fixed test keeps its signal.
When a model has defeated an evaluation, rebuild it by running the strongest available model to find where it starts struggling and making that failure point the new starting difficulty.

Verify a candidate evaluation's AI-resistance against the strongest available (including pre-release) model, not a casual run, and probe with extended thinking budgets and a test-time-compute harness before trusting it.

Accept the trade-off that strong AI-resistance conflicts with resembling the real job; when realism can no longer survive AI, an evaluation that simulates novel work can still carry valid hiring signal.
Run the evaluation in a realistic, unobserved environment (candidate's own editor, no narration) and allocate time for understanding existing systems and building tooling.
Have colleagues who are less steeped in the specific problem confirm that humans can still outperform the model, so the signal is not an artifact of the designer's own expertise.

Prefer novel, sufficiently out-of-distribution problems and avoid topics for which the model has abundant training data (e.g. common optimization patterns), because human reasoning wins over the model only where its prior experience base is thin.
When the role itself involves working with AI, explicitly permit AI tools in the evaluation and use longer-horizon problems so candidates must still demonstrate their own skill.
Do not attempt to ban AI assistance as your AI-resistance strategy: it is hard to enforce and does not reflect a job where people work with AI.
Do not define success as 'substantially outperform the model alone', because that makes passively watching the model the dominant strategy once the model works faster than a human can read and steer.

Design for high signal: avoid single-insight problems, give many independent chances to demonstrate ability, aim for a wide scoring distribution, and include more depth than even strong candidates can finish.

Choose a time horizon long enough to reflect real work (on the order of hours) but balance it against candidate burden and pipeline overhead; shorten it when the remaining depth still distinguishes candidates.
Avoid requiring narrow or specific domain knowledge; test fundamentals that transfer, so the candidate pool is not needlessly restricted.
Make the evaluation engaging, representative of real work, and enjoyable (fast dev loops, depth, room for creativity) to raise participation and resolution of signal.
Use candidates' tooling investment as signal: withhold visualization/debugging tools or include a bug to fix, so building tools and judging how much to invest becomes part of what is measured.
Remove problem elements the current model has already fully solved, since they add no discriminating signal and only slow the development loop.
Prefer an evaluation composed of several independent sub-problems to reduce variance relative to a single deep problem.
Trust a well-designed take-home over paper credentials: it lets strong candidates with limited formal experience demonstrate real skill.

Always give Claude a check it can run itself (tests, build, linter, fixture diff, or screenshot comparison) so it can iterate to a pass/fail signal and close the loop without a human as the verification step.

Match the stop-gate strength to the stakes: iterate in one prompt, a /goal condition, a deterministic Stop hook, or a verification subagent — noting a Stop hook is overridden after 8 consecutive blocks.

Separate exploration and planning from implementation, and scale planning to task size: act directly on small clear-scope changes, but plan when the approach is uncertain, the change spans multiple files, or the code is unfamiliar.
Reserve vague, open-ended prompts for exploratory work where you can afford to course-correct, to surface issues you would not have thought to ask about.
Reduce permission-prompt friction with the least-privilege option that fits: auto mode, allowlists for known-safe commands, or OS-level sandboxing.
Prefer CLI tools (gh, aws, gcloud) for external services because they are the most context-efficient interface, and install the gh CLI to avoid unauthenticated rate limits.
Use Claude Code as an onboarding aid by asking it senior-engineer-level questions about an unfamiliar codebase.

For large features, have Claude interview you (AskUserQuestion) into a self-contained SPEC.md that names files/interfaces, states out-of-scope, and ends with end-to-end verification, then execute it in a fresh session.

Course-correct as soon as Claude drifts (Esc, /rewind, 'undo that'), and after more than two failed corrections on the same issue, /clear and restart with a better prompt rather than accumulating a polluted context.
Use rewind checkpoints to attempt risky approaches and restore conversation and/or code, while remembering checkpoints track only Claude's own changes and are not a substitute for git.
Treat sessions like branches: name them with /rename and resume with --continue/--resume so each workstream keeps its own persistent context.

Multiply throughput and improve review quality by running multiple sessions in parallel (worktrees, desktop, web, agent teams), including a Writer/Reviewer split so review happens in a fresh context not biased toward the code just written.
Fan out large migrations or analyses by looping claude -p over tasks with --allowedTools scoping permissions for batch operations.
Run long unattended work in auto mode (claude --permission-mode auto -p), aware that in non-interactive -p runs it aborts when the classifier repeatedly blocks actions.
Treat these best-practice patterns as adaptable defaults rather than fixed rules: deviate deliberately when a task warrants it, and build intuition by noticing what makes Claude succeed or struggle.

Configure container resources with a guaranteed allocation and a separate, higher hard-kill limit; never pin both to the same value, since zero headroom lets a transient memory spike OOM-kill a container that would otherwise have passed.

Calibrate the resource floor-to-ceiling band so scores at the floor and at the ceiling fall within noise of each other, and report the chosen multiplier because the right value varies by benchmark and task distribution.

Separate infrastructure-reliability gains from capability gains: added headroom up to roughly 3x mainly removes transient-spike failures without making the eval easier, whereas headroom beyond that lets agents solve tasks they otherwise could not and changes what the eval measures, so keep resource pressure in the reliability band.

When comparing models, hold the entire runtime constant (same harness, task set, and hardware for both scaffold and inference stack); agents given different resource budgets or time limits are not taking the same test.

Benchmark maintainers should publish both recommended per-task resource specs and the enforcement methodology (guaranteed-allocation versus hard-kill semantics); specs without enforcement detail leave a reproducibility gap.

When consuming leaderboards, treat agentic-eval differences below about 3 percentage points as within uncertainty until the configuration is documented and matched, since infrastructure confounders stack on top of binomial confidence intervals and the extremes of the allocation range reach about 6 points.

Account for model-strategy interaction with resources: because models differ in default approaches (heavyweight dependency installs versus lean from-scratch implementations), a fixed resource limit favors some models' defaults, so document the configuration to make that bias visible.

Expect the resource-headroom effect to generalize in direction but not magnitude across models and benchmarks (replicated across Anthropic models and on SWE-bench with a smaller effect on less resource-intensive tasks), so do not assume one benchmark's calibration transfers unchanged.
Keep the optional license field short, using either a license name or a reference to a bundled license file.
Only add the compatibility field when the skill has specific environment requirements, and keep it within 1-500 characters when present.
Model the optional metadata field as a string-to-string map and give its keys reasonably unique names to avoid conflicts with other clients.
Make scripts self-contained or explicitly document their dependencies, emit helpful error messages, handle edge cases, and remember that supported script languages depend on the agent implementation.
When the agent repeatedly reinvents the same logic across runs, write that logic once as a tested script and bundle it in scripts/ rather than relying on the agent to regenerate it.

For reusable logic, bundle a self-contained script that declares its dependencies inline (PEP 723 for Python, npm:/jsr: for Deno, runtime auto-install for Bun, bundler/inline for Ruby) so the agent runs it in one command with no separate manifest or install step, while accounting for each mechanism's caveats.

Document the script interface with concise --help output (description, flags, usage examples) and distinct, documented exit codes, since that output is how an agent learns and disambiguates the interface.
Validate a skill with the skills-ref library to confirm its SKILL.md frontmatter is valid and follows the naming conventions before shipping.
State a skill's prerequisites explicitly in SKILL.md rather than assuming the agent's environment provides them, using the compatibility frontmatter field for runtime-level requirements.

Give every SKILL.md the required frontmatter: a lowercase, hyphenated name field (typically matching the directory) and a description field stating what the skill does and when to use it; license is optional.

Write skills as reusable procedures that teach how to approach a class of problems, not as declarations that hard-code the answer for one specific instance, so the approach generalizes even when details are specific.

Maintain a gotchas section in SKILL.md itself listing concrete, environment-specific corrections (not generic advice); add a new gotcha whenever the agent makes a mistake you have to correct, because a separate file may not be loaded at the moment the trigger occurs.

Specify required output formats with concrete templates rather than prose descriptions (agents pattern-match structures well); keep short templates inline and store longer or conditional ones in assets/ referenced from SKILL.md so they load only when needed.
Give multi-step workflows an explicit checklist so the agent tracks progress and does not skip steps, especially when steps have dependencies or validation gates.

Design a small, varied, realistic test set: begin with 2-3 cases, vary phrasing/detail/formality, include at least one edge or boundary case, and ground every prompt in realistic context (file paths, column names) rather than vague instructions.
Interview for edge cases, input/output formats, example files, success criteria, and dependencies -- and do any available MCP or subagent research -- before writing test prompts.

Capture per-run token count and duration and treat output quality against time/token cost as an explicit trade-off; in Claude Code, save total_tokens and duration_ms from the completion notification immediately because they are not persisted elsewhere.
Capture each run's total_tokens and duration_ms to timing.json the moment the task-completion notification arrives, because that is the only opportunity -- the data is not persisted anywhere else.

Write assertions that are verifiable, specific, or countable and avoid vague or brittle ones (e.g. exact-phrase matches); leave subjective qualities like style and visual design to human review instead of forcing them into pass/fail checks.

While runs are in progress, draft objectively-verifiable, descriptively-named assertions (judge subjective skills qualitatively instead of forcing assertions), and check any programmatically-verifiable assertion with a written, reusable script rather than by eye.

Grade each assertion PASS or FAIL with concrete evidence that references the output, requiring real substance and never giving the benefit of the doubt — a correct label with missing substance is a FAIL.

Use verification scripts for mechanically checkable assertions (valid JSON, row counts, file dimensions) and reserve LLM grading for judgement calls, because scripts are more reliable and reusable across iterations.

Continuously QA the assertions themselves: remove assertions that pass in both configurations (no signal, inflated pass rate), fix or investigate assertions that fail in both, and mine assertions that pass with the skill but fail without it to learn where the skill adds value.

Aggregate per-configuration statistics (pass_rate, time, tokens) plus a delta into benchmark.json and read the delta as cost-versus-benefit; treat standard deviation as meaningful only when there are multiple runs per eval.

Drive skill iteration from three combined signals — failed assertions, human feedback, and execution transcripts — by giving all three plus the current SKILL.md to an LLM and asking it to propose improvements.
Generalize fixes to address underlying issues broadly rather than adding narrow patches for specific test cases, because the skill will run across many unseen prompts.
Keep the skill lean — favour fewer, better instructions — and if pass rates plateau despite adding rules, treat it as over-constrained and try removing instructions.
Exempt skill content from context compaction and pruning, because silently losing durable skill instructions mid-session degrades performance with no visible error.

Improve by generalizing from the handful of iteration examples to the skill's many future uses: strip instructions that are not earning their place (read the run transcripts, not just the final outputs), avoid overfitted fixes and constrictive MUSTs, treat all-caps ALWAYS/NEVER and rigid structure as a yellow flag to reframe with explained reasoning, and bundle any helper script that multiple runs independently reinvent under scripts/.
Prefer reasoning-based instructions ('do X because Y causes Z') over rigid directives ('ALWAYS/NEVER'), because models follow instructions more reliably when they understand the purpose.
Bundle repeated helper work into the skill's scripts/ directory when multiple runs independently reimplement the same helper.
Do not rely on a skill triggering for simple one-step requests; expect activation mainly on non-trivial tasks that exceed what the agent can do with basic tools alone.
Keep skills minimal and well-scoped: put the actionable instructions the agent will follow (and adapt to request parameters) in the body, favoring a compact single-file skill over verbose ones.
Write descriptions in imperative 'Use this skill when...' phrasing framed on user intent and the goal the user is pursuing, not on the skill's internal implementation or mechanics.

Keep the description concise (a few sentences to a short paragraph) and always within the 1024-character hard limit, re-checking the length after every optimization pass since descriptions tend to grow.

Select the final description by its validation-set pass rate rather than by taking the last iteration, then verify it with manual sanity checks and 5-10 fresh queries never used during optimization before shipping.
Build a labeled eval set of realistic user prompts (about 20 queries, roughly balanced 8-10 should-trigger and 8-10 should-not-trigger) before attempting to improve a description.

When optimizing a description, build about 20 realistic, concrete, detailed trigger eval queries split between should-trigger and should-not-trigger cases, and make the negatives genuine near-misses (shared keywords, different actual need) rather than obviously irrelevant queries that test nothing.
Design should-trigger queries that vary across phrasing, explicitness, detail, and complexity, favoring cases where the skill helps but the connection is not obvious from the query alone.

Revise by failure direction: broaden scope or add usefulness context when should-trigger queries miss, and add specificity or clarify boundaries with adjacent skills when should-not-trigger queries false-fire — without copying keywords from the failed queries.

Design eval queries around how triggering actually works: Claude consults a skill only for tasks it cannot easily handle itself, so simple one-step queries may fail to trigger even a well-matched skill while complex, multi-step, or specialized queries trigger reliably -- make eval queries substantive enough to genuinely benefit from a skill.
Prioritize near-miss negative queries that share keywords or concepts with the skill but actually need something different; obviously-irrelevant negatives add little diagnostic value.
Measure triggering empirically by running each query with the skill installed, observing invocation via client logs or tool-call histories, and scoring each result against its expected label.
Because triggering is nondeterministic, run each query multiple times (about three) and decide pass/fail on a trigger rate against a threshold (about 0.5), rather than on a single run.

Guard against overfitting with a fixed, proportionally-stratified train (~60%) / validation (~40%) split, and let only train-set failures drive description revisions while validation is reserved to check generalization.

If iterative refinement stalls after several passes (around five is usually enough), switch to a structurally different description framing instead of incremental tweaks, and suspect the eval queries if performance still will not improve.

Match command form to complexity: reference an existing package as a one-off command for simple few-flag invocations, and promote it to a tested script under scripts/ once it becomes complex or hard to get right.
Pin tool and dependency versions (tool@version, PEP 508 specifiers, lockfiles such as uv lock --script) so command behaviour is reproducible over time.

Never require interactive input in a script: agents run in non-interactive shells and cannot answer TTY prompts, so accept all input via command-line flags, environment variables, or stdin to avoid indefinite hangs.
Write error messages that state what went wrong, what was expected, and what to try, because an opaque error wastes an agent turn and shapes its next attempt.
Emit structured output (JSON, CSV, or TSV) on stdout and send progress, warnings, and other diagnostics to stderr so the agent and standard tools get clean, parseable data.
Make scripts idempotent and retry-safe, preferring create-if-not-exists over create-and-fail-on-duplicate, because agents may retry commands.
Reject ambiguous input with a clear error rather than guessing, and constrain inputs with enums or closed sets.
Make the skill's name a short identifier that exactly matches its containing folder name.

Name every skill using only lowercase letters, numbers, and hyphens, match the SKILL.md 'name' to its parent directory name, keep it under 64 characters, and never add slashes, colons, dots, or namespace prefixes — invalid names make the skill silently fail to load.
When updating an existing skill rather than creating one, preserve its original name and directory and edit a copy in a writeable location, since the installed path may be read-only.

Discover all available skills at session startup and load their metadata, scanning at least the project-level (working directory) and user-level (home directory) scopes, plus any further scopes the deployment model requires.

Identify a skill as any subdirectory containing a file named exactly 'SKILL.md', skip non-skill directories such as '.git/' and 'node_modules/', and bound the scan (e.g. max depth 4-6, a directory cap) to prevent runaway traversal.

Adapt discovery to sandboxed/cloud agents: project-level skills travel with a cloned repo and can be scanned from its tree, user-level and organization-level skills must be provisioned externally, and built-in skills can ship as static deployment assets.
Parse each SKILL.md by splitting YAML frontmatter (between '---' delimiters) from the markdown body, extracting the required name and description plus any optional fields.

Validate skill metadata leniently: warn but still load on cosmetic issues (name/directory mismatch, name over 64 characters), but skip and log the skill when the description is missing/empty or the YAML is completely unparseable.
A SKILL.md must carry a name and a description in its YAML frontmatter plus markdown instructions; a compatibility field for tools/dependencies is optional and rarely needed.

Tolerate technically-invalid YAML authored for other clients (commonly unquoted values containing colons) with a fallback that quotes such values or converts them to block scalars before retrying, to improve cross-client compatibility.

Place the catalog as a labeled system-prompt section or embedded in a dedicated activation tool's description, and accompany it with a concise behavioral-instruction block that matches the supported activation mechanism.
Rely on model-driven activation — the model judging relevance from the catalog — rather than harness-side keyword or trigger matching.

Support activation by file-read (simplest when the model can read files) and/or a dedicated activation tool (required when it cannot, and useful otherwise for content control, structured wrapping, resource listing, permission enforcement, and analytics).
Create a custom skill specifically when a task must be performed in a specific, repeatable way.
Bootstrap skills with AI rather than authoring from scratch — use /create-skill from a description, or extract a reusable skill from a completed conversation that solved a multi-step problem.

Use MCP servers to give Copilot access to external systems, APIs, databases, and real-time data (e.g. GitHub MCP for issues/PRs, Playwright MCP for browser testing); configure via mcp.json, repository MCP settings on GitHub, or a custom agent's mcp-servers property.

Before promising a customization feature works on a given IDE or surface, verify it against the feature-support matrix and recommend the latest stable IDE/CLI/extension versions, because support varies per surface and some features are only preview or unsupported (e.g. hooks are not in Visual Studio/JetBrains/Eclipse/Xcode; prompt files are not in Eclipse/GitHub.com/Copilot CLI; only MCP servers are supported everywhere).

When advising JetBrains IDE users, direct them to the Agent Customizations editor (Copilot Chat panel settings, then Customizations) to view/edit custom agents, manage skills, configure instructions, manage prompt files, and choose Workspace (project) versus Personal (cross-project) scope.
After adding or changing a skill during a CLI session, run /skills reload and confirm with /skills info SKILL-NAME before relying on the skill.

Prefer judgement-anchored guidance over rigid rules for newer-generation models: point the model at surrounding context instead of hard-coding not-always-true rules, since capable models handle the decision well without them.

Invest heavily in the system prompt when building your own agent harness, since it carries the product context (what product the agent is in and what it does); Claude Code's own system prompt is rarely modified by users.
Rely on automatic memory for durable, relevant context instead of manually writing memories into CLAUDE.md.
Periodically simplify and rightsize the system prompt, skills, and CLAUDE.md, and use the Claude Code 'claude doctor' / /doctor command to automate much of that rightsizing.

Match wording to the user's demonstrated technical familiarity: gate jargon such as 'JSON' and 'assertion' on clear cues the user knows them, treat 'evaluation' and 'benchmark' as borderline, and briefly define terms when in doubt.

After drafting, write two to three realistic, real-user-language test prompts, get the user's sign-off, and save them to evals/evals.json without assertions (assertions are added later, while runs are in progress).
Emit grading results using exactly the fields text, passed, and evidence, because the results viewer depends on those exact field names.

Generate the eval viewer with generate_review.py rather than hand-written HTML (use its --static option in headless/no-display environments), and put it in front of the human to review before you evaluate any outputs yourself.
Treat empty user feedback as approval, and concentrate revisions on the specific test cases the user actually complained about.
Continue the improve-rerun-review loop until the user is satisfied, all feedback is empty, or you stop making meaningful progress.
Run the description-optimization loop with the exact model ID powering the current session, so the triggering test matches what the user actually experiences.

Rely on the optimizer's built-in discipline -- a 60/40 train/held-out split, three repetitions per query for a reliable trigger rate, up to five iterations, and selection of best_description by test score -- and do not pick a description on train score alone, to avoid overfitting.

On Claude.ai (no subagents), run test cases yourself one at a time by following the SKILL.md, and skip baseline runs, quantitative benchmarking, and description optimization (which requires the claude CLI).

Bundle specialized subagent instructions under an agents/ directory (e.g. grader, comparator, analyzer) and JSON-shape documentation under references/schemas.md, reading each only when needed, and track the workflow steps on a TodoList -- in Cowork explicitly including a to-do to create the evals JSON and run the viewer before revising.
